lesson.subtitle: Lesson 16 -- Milestone Review
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Felipe Pimenta | Lesson 16 -- Milestone Review
lesson.grammar_point: future perfect and future perfect continuous

listenings.text: Felipe, it is Sarah Whitmore from Hartley and Vance. I left you almost exactly this message a year ago, so forgive the symmetry. Back then I told you about a payments company looking for a finance leader, you called me back, and you took thirty minutes in English. I remember thinking at the time that the English was the smaller obstacle. It usually is. I am calling because the same client has come back to me, and this time the role is bigger and the conversation is with the board rather than the chief executive. Four people, one hour, and at least one question designed to see how you think when you have not prepared. Here is my honest advice, and it is the same advice I give every senior candidate. Do not walk in there trying to sound perfect. Walk in there able to say what you do not know, in a full sentence, without apologizing for it. That is what a board reads as seniority. Call me back this week. And Felipe, listen to the first message again if you still have it. You will not recognize the man who answered it.

I run language programs for companies, and at the end of every one I get the same question. What happens now. So here is the honest answer. Nothing collapses in a week, but a skill you stop using does fade, and the part that fades first is not grammar. It is speed. You will still understand everything. You will simply take a second longer to produce it, and that second is what other people mistake for your level. So protect the speed, not the vocabulary. Fifteen minutes of speaking out loud, three times a week, does more than two hours of reading. Record yourself once a month and keep the files, because progress at this stage is far too slow to feel and far too obvious to miss on two recordings six months apart. And find one room where you are the least fluent person present, and walk into it on purpose. Comfort is where a plateau begins. One last thing, and it is the one that matters. Do not measure yourself against a native speaker. They are not the benchmark and they never were. Measure yourself against the recording you made on your first day. That is the only comparison that has ever told anybody the truth.

reading.rtitle: The Recording He Never Played Back
paras: On the first evening of the program he recorded three minutes about himself and never played the file back. It was, by every account including his own, painful: long silences, a sentence started three times, and a vocabulary that ran out exactly where the interesting part began. Had anyone told him that evening that he would one day chair a quarterly call in English, he would have laughed. What he did not understand at the time was that the recording was not a verdict on him. It was a baseline.

Sixteen sessions later the same man opened the same file and could not finish it. Not because it was bad, but because it was somebody else. He has since said that the strangest part was hearing how hard he once had to work for sentences that are now second nature. If he had kept a diary, he says, he would be able to point at the week it turned; but nothing turned in a week. The gain was incremental, which is precisely why he could not feel it while it was happening. Nobody notices the moment a plateau ends.

His teacher had him record the same three minutes again on the last evening — same prompt, same clock, no notes. He was told to speak off the cuff, and he did. There were still mistakes; there always are. But he held his own for three minutes, he asked two questions back, and he closed on a number. His blind spot, he now admits, was never grammar. It was the half-second of silence he used to fill with an apology, and which he now fills with a line he can fall back on: give me a second, let me put that another way.

He would be the first to say that a course does not finish anything. By this time next year he will have been leading in English for eighteen months, and by the time the next audit committee meets he will have presented four sets of results in a language that was, not long ago, the reason he stayed quiet. That is not fluency arriving one morning. It is a benchmark moving — slowly, and then all at once — because somebody was willing to be recorded badly on a Tuesday and to keep the file.
reading.source: Case study -- Corporate language program, exit review

gist.prompt: Which summary survives the fourth paragraph?
choices: He improved because he finally learned enough vocabulary to stop making mistakes in front of other people.
The change was incremental and invisible week by week; what the two recordings show is not perfect English arriving, but a baseline that moved and a silence he now fills instead of apologizing for.
He made progress only because his teacher forced him to record himself a second time at the end of the course.

items: He listened back to his first recording several times during the program.

guiding.title: Talk it through
items: He could not finish listening to his own first recording. If you played yours right now, what do you think you would hear first?
His blind spot was the half-second of silence he filled with an apology. What do you still fill yours with — and what could you fall back on instead?
He measures himself against his own first day, not against a native speaker. Say out loud what will already be true for you by this time next year.

items.situation: A board member asks about a decision that went wrong three years ago.
tips: If we had seen the pricing issue earlier, we would not have taken the write-off.
The regret sits entirely in the past: third conditional.

items.situation: You have fifteen minutes and four strangers, and nobody in the room knows where you are taking them.
tips: I will take you through three things: where we are, what changed, and what I need from you.
Signposting. Name the map before the journey, not during it.

items.situation: You disagree with the chief executive in front of his own board.
tips: I take your point, and I would want to flag one risk before we commit to that.
Hedge first, then land the objection. Never the reverse.

items.situation: A recruiter asks you to describe a time you turned something around.
tips: The division was losing money; the pricing model was the root cause; I rebuilt it in a quarter; margin went from minus three to plus six.
STAR, and finish on the number.

items.situation: Someone asks whether you will be ready for the board meeting on the fourteenth.
tips: By the fourteenth I will have presented these numbers four times.
Future perfect: stand at the deadline and look back at what is already done.

items.situation: The line is bad and you have lost the last sentence completely.
tips: Sorry, I lost you there. Could you give me that last part again?
Ask cleanly. Apologize for the line, never for your English.
